---
title: "Testing the Design"
---

## Why This Matters

You've built something. It works, at least on your machine. But you do not know whether it solves your users' problem until you watch real people try to use it.

**The model:** give about five real users a real task and watch what they do. Behavior shows the problem; opinions hide it. Fix the worst problem, then test again.

This chapter teaches you to run a usability test, synthesize what you saw without overreacting, and then fix the problems and test again.

This is triangulation from [Finding and Validating the Problem](04-finding-and-validating-the-problem.qmd) in practice. One user shows you one partial view of the problem. Watch enough of them and the full problem appears. No single tester, however loud or however pleased, is proof on their own.

<!-- learn -->

## The Curse of Knowledge

You built this thing. You know exactly where every button is, what every label means, why the workflow goes left to right. Your users don't. They're seeing it for the first time, bringing different mental models, and expecting it to work like other things they've used (Jakob's Law, from [Interface and Flow](05-interface-and-flow.qmd)).

This is the **curse of knowledge**: once you know something, it's nearly impossible to imagine not knowing it [@heath2007stick]. The only way around it is to watch people who don't know.

The same curse applies to the agent that built your app. It knows what every element was meant to do, so asking it "is this usable?" gets you the builder's view. It can review your screens against principles; it cannot be a first-time user.

<!-- learn -->

## The Design Canon Behind This

Two ideas from design shape what you are testing for. Don Norman's *The Design of Everyday Things* [@norman2013design] gives you **affordances** and **signifiers**: good design makes the right action obvious, a door you push has a plate, a door you pull has a handle. When users hesitate, a signifier is usually missing. Steve Krug's *Don't Make Me Think* [@krug2014think] gives you the standard to test against: every moment a user has to stop and figure out your interface is friction you can remove.

This matters more with AI. It will generate a screen that *looks* polished in seconds, but polish is not usability, and a good-looking interface can still make people think. Watching real users is exactly what reveals the difference, and no AI can do it in your place.

*From Don Norman, The Design of Everyday Things (first published 1988; revised edition 2013), and Steve Krug, Don't Make Me Think (first published 2000; revised edition 2014).*

<!-- learn -->

## What is Usability Testing?

Usability testing is observing real users attempt to accomplish real tasks with your product. It's not a demo. It's not a survey. It's watching someone struggle (or succeed) while you stay quiet and take notes.

**What usability testing reveals:**
- Where users get stuck or confused
- What they expect vs. what they get
- Whether users understand your core value proposition
- What terminology confuses them
- Which features they ignore completely

**What usability testing doesn't reveal:**
- Whether they'll pay for it (that's validation)
- Whether the market is big enough (that's research)
- What features to build next (that's strategy)

#### Why five users

Jakob Nielsen's rule of thumb, from a model he built with Thomas Landauer [@nielsen1993mathematical], is that a test with about five users finds most of the usability problems in a design, around 85 percent in his [2000 summary](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-you-only-need-to-test-with-5-users/). The building blocks of the argument:

- Each user runs into some share of the problems. The first user shows you a lot you did not know.
- Each additional user mostly repeats problems you have already seen, so new findings fall off fast.
- So the better use of fifteen sessions is three rounds of five, with a fix between each round. Fixes can fail or create new problems, and only a retest shows that.

![New findings fall off fast: five users find about 85 percent of the problems, and the next ten mostly repeat them. Fifteen sessions find more as three rounds of five with a fix between. Curve after Nielsen and Landauer's model [@nielsen1993mathematical].](images/diagrams/ch06-five-users.svg){#fig-five-users fig-alt="A line chart of the share of usability problems found against users tested, from 0 to 15. The curve rises steeply, reaches about 85 percent at five users, which is highlighted, and flattens toward 100 percent; the region from 6 to 15 users is shaded and labeled Users 6 to 15 mostly repeat what you have seen. Below, three boxes of five user icons labeled Round 1, Round 2, and Round 3 are joined by arrows labeled Fix." width="100%"}

The rule assumes your testers are the same kind of user. If you have two very different groups (students who post shifts and managers who approve them, say), test three or four from each.

An analogy: proofreading. The first fresh reader catches many of the typos; the fifth mostly finds the same ones. Where it breaks: typos are visible to anyone, while a usability problem only appears to someone with the user's goal and background, which is why the testers have to be real users.

## Running a Usability Test

#### Before the Session

1. **Define your goals**: What questions are you trying to answer?
2. **Prepare 3-5 tasks**: Specific things you want them to try, written as a goal ("Get your Thursday shift covered"), never as instructions ("Click Give away")
3. **Recruit the right people**: They should match your target user
4. **Set up recording**: Screen + audio (get permission)
5. **Prepare your script**: Consistent intro and task instructions

#### The Test Script Structure

```
INTRO (2 minutes)
"Thanks for helping me test this. I'm trying to improve [product],
and watching you use it helps me find problems. I'm testing the
product, not you, there are no wrong answers. Please think out loud
as you go. I'll mostly stay quiet and take notes."

WARM-UP (2 minutes)
"Tell me a little about yourself. Have you ever [relevant experience]?"

TASKS (15-20 minutes)
"Imagine you want to [scenario]. Go ahead and try to do that."
[Stay quiet. Observe. Take notes.]

FOLLOW-UP (5 minutes)
"What was that experience like for you?"
"What was most confusing?"
"When you paused on [screen], what were you looking for?"

WRAP-UP (1 minute)
"Thank you so much. This was really helpful."
```

The follow-up questions ask about what just happened. Avoid "What would you change?": it invites a design opinion, and opinions are exactly what this method is built to get past.

#### During the Session

**Do:**
- Stay silent while they work
- Let them struggle (it's painful, but necessary)
- Take detailed notes on behavior, not just outcomes
- Note where they pause, click wrong things, or seem uncertain
- Ask "What are you thinking?" if they go quiet

**Don't:**
- Help them unless they're completely stuck
- Explain why something works that way
- Defend your design decisions
- Lead with questions like "Did you see the button in the corner?"
- Ask "Do you like it?" (opinions aren't data)

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it"}
**Find the mistakes** in this session transcript. The tester is trying to post a shift on ShiftSwap.

> Builder: "Okay, so to post a shift you'd tap Give Away, the green button at the bottom."
>
> Tester: "Oh, okay." *(taps it)* "Hm, what's 'eligible coworkers'?"
>
> Builder: "That's everyone trained on the same station. It's filtered by the database."
>
> Tester: "Got it. Yeah, this is nice."
>
> Builder: "Great, so you'd use it?"

Name at least three things the builder did that cost real information, and rewrite the task prompt so it gives a goal instead of the answer.
:::

## What to Observe

| Observe | What It Tells You |
|---------|-------------------|
| **Task completion** | Can they do the core thing? |
| **Time on task** | Is it faster or slower than expected? |
| **Error rate** | Where do mistakes happen? |
| **Recovery** | Can they fix their mistakes? |
| **Verbal comments** | What frustrates or delights them? |
| **Facial expressions** | Where do they show confusion? |
| **Click patterns** | What do they try first? |

Record what people **did** before what they **said**. A tester who says "this is easy" after three wrong taps has told you two things, and the taps are the reliable one. The states from [Interface and Flow](05-interface-and-flow.qmd) are good places to watch closely: the first empty screen, the wait while something loads, and any error.

<!-- learn -->

## Synthesizing Feedback

After a round of about five tests, you'll have a lot of notes. Time to find patterns.

#### The Affinity Mapping Process

1. **Write each observation on a sticky note** (or digital equivalent)
2. **Group similar observations together**
3. **Name each group** (these become your themes)
4. **Prioritize by frequency and severity**

Claude Code is useful here once the observing is done: paste in your notes and ask it to group them and count how many testers hit each problem. Check its grouping against your notes; it was not in the room.

#### Severity Scoring

| Severity | Description | Example |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| **Critical** | Users cannot complete core task | Can't sign up |
| **Major** | Task is difficult but possible | Takes 5 minutes to find main feature |
| **Minor** | Annoying but doesn't block | Date field rejects "10/14" the first time; user retypes it and continues |
| **Cosmetic** | Polish issue | Icon looks dated |

Severity depends on what a problem does to the task, not on what kind of problem it is. A confusing label on the core action ("Submit" where the user expected "Post shift") can be Critical if testers stop there. Words are interface.

**Fix critical and major issues first.** Don't let minor issues distract you from what matters.

#### Fix the top issue and retest

The loop is the point of the method:

1. Pick the one or two highest-severity problems.
2. Fix them, ideally with a precise prompt that names the problem and the principle (see [Directing an Agent on Design](05-interface-and-flow.qmd#directing-an-agent-on-design)).
3. Run the same tasks with a new round of users.
4. Check that the problem is gone and that the fix did not create a new one.

## Iteration Frameworks

#### The Build-Measure-Learn Loop [@ries2011lean]

```
BUILD → MEASURE → LEARN → BUILD → ...
```

Each cycle should be as fast as possible:
- **Build**: Make a small, testable change
- **Measure**: Observe users with the change
- **Learn**: Decide what to do next

**Common mistake:** Building too much before measuring. Ship smaller changes so you learn sooner. In usability terms, the retest loop above is one turn of this cycle.

<!-- MOVE: "When to Pivot vs. Persevere" belongs in discovery (ch04) or ch14 Measuring What Matters because it is a decision about value, not usability. Kept here because it is on the Oct 20 midterm. -->

#### When to Pivot vs. Persevere

**Consider pivoting when:**
- Users consistently don't understand the value
- The problem you're solving isn't painful enough
- Multiple users suggest a different core use case
- You've iterated 3+ times with no improvement

**Consider persevering when:**
- Users struggle but eventually succeed
- Issues are about UX, not core value
- Fixes are straightforward (labeling, placement)
- Users express desire for the product

#### Responding to Feedback Without Overreacting

Not all feedback is equal. One user's opinion isn't a mandate.

**Process feedback through these filters:**

1. **Frequency**: Did multiple people say this?
2. **Severity**: Does it block the core task?
3. **Source**: Is this from your target user?
4. **Alignment**: Does it fit your product vision?

**Signs that feedback is misleading:**
- "I would want..." (hypothetical)
- "My friend would love..." (secondhand)
- Feature requests without a problem statement
- Requests that conflict with your core value prop

**Useful responses to feedback:**
- "That's interesting, tell me more about when that would happen."
- "What are you trying to accomplish when you need that?"
- "How do you handle that today?"

## Testing at Scale

Once your product has users, you can test at scale:

| Method | Best For | Sample Size |
|--------|----------|-------------|
| **Usability testing** | Deep understanding | About 5 per round, repeated |
| **A/B testing** | Optimizing metrics | 1000+ users |
| **Surveys** | Broad sentiment | 100+ users |
| **Analytics** | Behavior patterns | All users |
| **Session replay** | Specific issues | As needed |
| **In-app feedback button** | Bugs and confusion, reported when they happen | Any user who clicks it |
| **Agent walk-through** | Steps where the app does something a user would not expect | Before each round with people |

<!-- REVIEW: the A/B (1000+) and survey (100+) sample sizes are rules of thumb with no source; the right A/B size depends on the effect you want to detect. Consider pointing to ch14 instead of giving a number. -->

**Start with usability testing.** You need qualitative insights before you can optimize quantitatively. Analytics and A/B testing come back in [Measuring What Matters](14-measuring-what-matters.qmd).

The last two rows suit a product built with agents. A feedback button that sends, along with the
user's sentence, the page they were on, a screenshot, and the recent errors gives an agent enough
to reproduce the problem without going back to the user. The Agent Team Kit's
[feedback loop spec](https://github.com/ai-foundry-byu/agent-team-kit/blob/main/docs/FEEDBACK-LOOP-SPEC.md) describes how to build one, and its
[`fix-bug`](https://github.com/ai-foundry-byu/agent-team-kit/blob/main/skills/fix-bug/SKILL.md) skill is the agent's side of it. An agent walk-through,
such as the kit's [`ux-critique`](https://github.com/ai-foundry-byu/agent-team-kit/blob/main/skills/ux-critique/SKILL.md) skill, has an agent use the app
in a browser, predict at each step what should happen, and record where the app does something
else. It is cheap enough to run before every round of testing. It does not replace the five users:
the agent already knows what the app is for, which is the curse of knowledge from the start of
this chapter.

A note on the [Peer Product Testing](00-assessments.qmd#peer-product-testing) assignment: classmates are useful testers for finding where an interface confuses a first-time user, but most are not your target user. Treat a peer test as practice and a first pass, and still test with real users before you trust a result about your market.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it"}
Plan your next round: write one task as a goal, name five testers who match your target user (and say why each one does), and write the one problem from your last test you expect to be gone after your fix. After the round, check the prediction.
:::

<!-- learn -->

## Key Concepts

- **Watch, do not ask**: behavior shows the problem; opinions hide it
- **Curse of Knowledge**: You can't see your product like new users do, and neither can the agent that built it
- **Affordances and signifiers**: design that makes the right action obvious (Norman)
- **Don't make me think**: every pause to figure out the interface is friction (Krug)
- **Usability Testing**: Observing users attempt tasks, not asking opinions
- **Think-aloud**: testers narrate as they work; you stay quiet
- **The five-user rule**: about five comparable users per round find most problems; run several small rounds (Nielsen)
- **Task Completion**: The core metric, can they do the thing?
- **Affinity mapping**: group observations into themes, then rank by frequency and severity
- **Severity Scoring**: Critical > Major > Minor > Cosmetic, judged by the effect on the task
- **Fix and retest**: fix the top issues, then run the same tasks with new users
- **Build-Measure-Learn**: Fast iteration cycles
- **Pivot vs. Persevere**: When to change direction vs. keep improving
